execution_notes.pdf_verification_log: Six PDF pages read as images to verify wording: p.3-4 (PDF 18-19), p.81 (PDF 109), p.132 (PDF 159), p.168 (PDF 196, negative check), p.175-176 (PDF 203-204), p.251 (PDF 277), p.267 (PDF 293). execution_notes.caption_attribution_finding: In the von Franz volume the illustration captions were written by the editor, Daryl Sharp, not by von Franz (stated in the Acknowledgements, p.6). This matters for three items. Every occurrence of 'Mercurius' in the book (pp. 86, 100, 129, 168, 247 - exactly the index entry) is in a caption; von Franz's own lecture text never uses the word. 'Green lion' occurs once, in the caption to illustration 30 (p.105). The only lapis|Christ rendering in the book is the caption to illustration 42 (p.148). Renderings drawn from captions are labelled as Sharp's below and are not counted as von Franz renderings.
execution_notes.standing_finding_v3: The v2 finding about idiom instability inside one author now has a second instance and a partial reversal. Edinger equates Christ and the Anthropos flatly in Ego and Archetype (p.132) after rendering the same relation as doctrine-plus-quaternity in the Mysterium Lectures; and he refuses the lapis-Christ equation in Ego and Archetype (p.267) after asserting it flatly in Anatomy (ch. 3). The instability is not a drift in one direction - the same author tightens and loosens the same idiom across books.
execution_notes.excluded: Aurora Consurgens treatise and the ARAS blurb, per the addendum. No web search. v1/v2 renderings not re-litigated except where the addendum's sub-tasks require it.

sentence_subject_answer.question: Does Ego and Archetype mark anything like the sentence-subject distinction - identity when predicated of the term itself, correspondence when predicated of its symbols?
sentence_subject_answer.answer: No, and the way it fails to is more informative than v1's null was. Edinger's own predications fall out along exactly the line v0.6 draws: the copula goes to the term-pair ('The Self ... is identical with the imago Dei', p. 3) and symbol language goes to the image ('It is expressed by certain typical symbolic images called mandalas', p. 4). But the two sentences are twenty lines apart in one section and he never remarks that the subject changed, never treats the difference as carrying any weight, and never returns to it in the mandala chapter 170 pages later. The Critical Dictionary does the same thing across three entries. So the distinction is present in the literature's usage and absent from its concepts.
